Even if the entire world, including the devas, were to come and terrify me,

“Bhikkhus, ‘four venomous snakes of fierce power and terrible poison’ is a designation for these four great elements.

“Monks, ‘an empty village’ is a designation for these six internal sense bases.

“Bhikkhus, ‘this shore, fraught with peril and fear’ is a designation for identity view (*sakkāya*).

"Thus, monks, among things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, the Tathāgata is indeed 'such' (tādī). And I declare that there is no other one more 'such' than such a one, nor anyone superior or more excellent than such a one.

The Commentary on the Mahāpadāna Sutta, concerning the Second Council.

Question: At the first council, during the recitation of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), Venerable Sir, the entire commentary on the Vinaya, the commentary on the Sīlakkhandhavagga of the Dīghanikāya, and the commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī of the Abhidhamma were compiled by the Elders who conducted the sixth council.
Now, however, at the second council, from the commentary on the Mahāvagga of the Dīghanikāya...
From this point on, the occasion for the recitation of the remaining commentaries as they have been established has arrived.

Therefore, we shall begin to provide the questions and answers for the commentary on the Mahāpadāna Sutta within the Mahāvagga, which was reached according to the preliminary duties of this second communal recitation (saṅgīti).
Friends, regarding the introduction to the Mahāpadāna Sutta...
How did the commentator explain the meaning of the phrase “in the Kareri hut”?
Answer: Regarding the meaning of the phrase “in the Kareri hut” as it occurs in the introduction to the Mahāpadāna Sutta:
“Kareri” is the name of the *varuṇa* tree; the Kareri pavilion is the hut belonging to that tree.

Because it stands at the gate, it is called "Kareri Hut. Just as it is called "Kosamba Hut" because it stands at the gate of the *kosamba* tree, so too was it described by the venerable commentator (*aṭṭhakathācariya*).
Regarding the phrase "at Kareri Hut": *karerī* is the name for the *varuṇa* tree.
The Kareri Pavilion stood at the door of that hut; therefore, it is called the "Kareri Hut. Just as there is the "Kosamba Hut" because it stands at the door of a *kosamba* tree.

It is said that within the Jeta Grove there were four great dwellings—the Kareri Hut, the Kosamba Hut, the Perfumed Chamber (*Gandhakuṭī*), and the Salala House—each of which was completed through the gift of one hundred thousand pieces of gold.
Among those, the Salaḷāgāra was built by King Pasenadi.

Regarding the phrase in the *Pubbenivāsa-pucchā*: "Right there, friends, in that very context, a discourse on the Dhamma connected with past lives arose"—how did the Master of the Aṭṭhakathā explain its meaning?

The Explanation: Regarding the meaning of the statement, "Right there, Bhante, in that very introduction, a discourse on the Dhamma connected with past lives arose," the phrase "connected with past lives" means it was delivered in conjunction with what is termed a "past life"—that is, the continuity of aggregates (khandha-santāna) that existed in the past, reckoned as "one birth," "two births," and so forth. "On the Dhamma" means...

Connected with the Dhamma. "Arose" means: "Oh, how wonderful is the knowledge of past lives of the One Possessing the Ten Powers! Regarding what is called "past lives," who recollects them and who does not?
Those with wrong views do not recollect; disciples, paccekabuddhas, and Buddhas do recollect. Which views [do they hold] as they recollect?
Even those who have reached the highest attainment and are proponents of the efficacy of kamma [recollect].
"They recollect exactly forty eons, but not beyond that"—thus it was stated by the Master of the Commentaries (*Aṭṭhakathācariya*).

"Connected with past lives" means: having been joined with "past lives," which consist of the continuity of aggregates (*khandhasantāna*) that existed in the past, reckoned as "one birth, two births," and so forth.
This concludes the section on the delimitation of eons.

Question: Venerable sir, in that *Mahāpadāna Sutta*, within the section on the summary and the nine sections of analysis, how did the Master of the Commentary explain the meaning of the term "Bhaddakappa" (Auspicious Aeon) in the first section, the Analysis of Aeons?

Answer: Venerable sir, in that *Mahāpadāna Sutta*, within the section on the summary and the nine sections of analysis, the meaning of the term "Bhaddakappa" in the first section, the Analysis of Aeons, is as follows: it is called "Bhaddakappa" because it is adorned by the arising of five Buddhas.
In the *Sundarakappa* and the *Sārakappa*, the Blessed One spoke thus while praising this eon (*kappa*).

Regarding this, the venerable commentator (*aṭṭhakathācariya*) has stated: "From the time our Blessed One first made his resolution (*abhinīhāra*), it is said that in no single interval—nor even in a single eon—have five Buddhas ever appeared simultaneously. And so forth.
“Monks, in the ninety-first aeon from now, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, appeared in the world.

Because this aeon was adorned by the arising of five Buddhas, it was called the ‘Aeon of Sounds’ (*saddakappa*), a beautiful aeon (*sundarakappa*), a noble aeon (*sārakappa*). Honoring this aeon, the Blessed One spoke thus:
‘Indeed, from the time our Blessed One made his initial resolve, not even a single Buddha has arisen in any other aeon during that interval.’”
**The Section on the Limit of Life:
Question** Regarding the fourth section on the limit of life, venerable friend, how did the commentator explain the meaning of these words: "or a little more"?
**Answer** Regarding the fourth section on the limit of life, venerable sir, as for these words "or a little more": [the commentary explains them as follows:]...
The meaning is: "A little more" means less than a hundred years;
that is, one lives for twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty years, without reaching another hundred. However, such a long life is extremely rare;
one must go here and there to see someone, thinking, "It is said that such-and-such a person lives this long."
Thus it was stated there by the commentator, venerable sir.
"Monks, at present my lifespan is short, limited, and brief; whoever lives long lives for a hundred years or a little more.
'A little more' means that beyond a hundred years it is still little—noble sirs, without reaching a full hundred years, one lives for twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty years."

**The Section on the Delimitation of Attendants** **Question:** But in the eighth section, the "Delimitation of Attendants," how is Ānanda described by the commentator? **Answer:** Regarding the eighth section, the "Delimitation of Attendants," the commentator describes it as follows:
"But 'Ānanda' is said with reference to his status as a permanent attendant," and so forth. Thus, venerable sir, he is described by the commentator.
"Monks, at present Ānanda is my attendant, my chief attendant.

at times Nāgasamāla would wander about carrying his bowl and robes."

But when, Pañcasikha, were these verses of yours—concerning the Buddha, concerning the Dhamma, concerning the Saṅgha, concerning the Arahants, and concerning sensual pleasures—composed?
Thinking that no opportunity had been granted by the Blessed One to Pañcasikha, the deity would have turned back from that very spot and departed.
Consequently, he would have become greatly deprived. However, when his praise was spoken, [he realized] that an opportunity had indeed been granted by the Blessed One to Pañcasikha;
thus, having approached together with the deities, he asked a question, and at the conclusion of the answer, together with eighty thousand deities...
Knowing that he would be established in the fruit of stream-entry, the Blessed One spoke words of praise.

Then the Blessed One said this to Sakka, the lord of the devas: "It is wonderful, venerable Kosiya; it is marvelous, venerable Kosiya, that you have come here despite having so many duties and so much to do.
"Venerable sir, for a long time I have desired to approach the Blessed One to see him; however, [I was occupied] with the Tāvatiṃsa devas..."
Being occupied with various duties and tasks, I was unable to approach the Blessed One for a visit.

Those [gods], being unable to decide whether [the flowers] belonged to you or to me, engaged in a dispute and questioned Sakka, the king of the gods. He said, "They belong to whichever one's mansion they are closer to.
He further said, "They belong to whichever one she stood looking at while her mansion was visible."
"Right here in Kapilavatthu, venerable sir, there was a daughter of the Sakyans named Gopikā.
She had faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dhamma, and faith in the Saṅgha; she practiced the precepts in their entirety.
Having discarded her femininity and developed masculinity, with the breakup of the body, after death, she was reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world."
"It is for the sake of attaining that Dhamma, O Noble One, that we have come;
having been granted leave by the Blessed One, O Noble One, let us ask our question.
"Ask me your question, Vāsava, whatever you desire in your mind."
"I shall bring you to the end of each and every question.
"What, dear sir, are the fetters of the gods, humans, asuras, nāgas, gandhabbas, and whatever other diverse beings there may be, such that they think:
'May we dwell free from enmity, free from weapons, free from hostility, free from affliction, saying, "May we live without enemies"? And yet...
"But those who dwell with enmity, with violence, with hostility, and with ill will, thinking 'we have enemies,' [suffer].
However, O Lord of the Devas, for the gods, humans, asuras, nāgas, gandhabbas, and whatever other diverse beings there are who are bound by the fetters of envy and stinginess, they think:
'May we dwell without enmity, without violence, without hostility, and without ill will, thinking "we have no enemies. And this is their thought."
"And yet they dwell with enmity, with violence, with hostility, and with malice;

thus they are 'possessing enmity'. *Issā* (envy) means *issati* (one envies). Its characteristic is the grudging of others' prosperity. Its function is dissatisfaction with that very [prosperity]. It is manifested as turning away from it. Its proximate cause is the prosperity of others. It should be regarded as a fetter (*saṃyojana*). *Mācchariya* (avarice) is the state of being avaricious.
Its characteristic is the concealment of one's own prosperity—whether already obtained or yet to be obtained.
It should be understood as having the essence of intolerance for the sharing of those very things with others; its manifestation is shrinking back, or its manifestation is harshness and resentment;
its proximate cause is one's own excellence; and it is to be seen as a deformity of the mind.
As for the question "What is his appearance?", one who speaks of such and such faults and does not impart any portion of the scriptures to anyone becomes both ugly and dull-witted.
As long as that [craving] is not abandoned, even though gods and humans may aspire to freedom from enmity and so forth, they are still not released from enmity and the rest.
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, asked the Blessed One a further question:

"But, dear sir, what is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, and what is the provenance of envy and avarice? When what exists do envy and avarice come to be? When what does not exist do envy and avarice not come to be?"
"Lord of the Devas, envy and avarice have what is dear and what is not dear as their source, their origin, their birth, and their provenance.
When there is what is dear and what is not dear, envy and avarice arise; when there is nothing dear or not dear, envy and avarice do not exist.
[One practices avarice] by saying such things as, "It cannot be given," or "He will become weary," or "He will become dissatisfied."
One harbors envy, thinking: "Alas, may such a thing not happen to him.
One harbors stinginess, thinking: "We too claim this as our own; we do not enjoy it, nor can we give it away.
Or one harbors envy, thinking: "Who else besides me is a recipient of such a gain? Or, when asked, one harbors stinginess by refusing to give even for a limited time.

"But, dear sir, what is the source of the pleasant and the unpleasant? What is their origin, what is their birth, what is their provenance? When what exists does the pleasant and the unpleasant come to be? When what does not exist does the pleasant and the unpleasant not come to be?

"The pleasant and the unpleasant, lord of the devas, have desire as their source, desire as their origin, desire as their birth, desire as their provenance. When desire exists, the pleasant and the unpleasant come to be; when desire does not exist, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not come to be."

In this context, *chanda-nidāna* (the source of desire) refers to fivefold desire: the desire for seeking, the desire for acquisition, the desire for enjoyment, the desire for hoarding, and the desire for giving away.
[Thinking: "These will protect me, they will guard me, they will cherish me, they will surround me"—such is desire.
Now, dear sir, what is the source of desire, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its provenance? When what exists does desire come to be?
"When what is absent does desire not arise? "Lord of the Devas, desire has its source in thought, its origin in thought, it is born of thought, and it arises from thought.
When thought is present, desire arises; when thought is absent, desire does not arise.
"There will be this much of form, this much of sound, this much of smell, this much of taste..."
"There will be this much for touch; there will be this much for me; there will be this much for another; I shall store up this much;
I shall give this much to another"—such a determination arises through the investigation of thought.
Therefore it was said: "Desire, O Lord of Devas, has thought as its source."
"But how, dear sir, is a bhikkhu practicing the way that leads to the cessation of the conceptual proliferations of perception?
"O Lord of Devas, I say that joy is of two kinds: that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.
O Lord of Devas, I say that grief is of two kinds: that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated. O Lord of Devas, I say that equanimity is [likewise]..."
"I say that there are two kinds: those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated.
"But was it asked by the Blessed One, or was it spoken unasked? Was it with a coherent sequence, or without a sequence?
"It was spoken only when asked, not unasked; it was with a coherent sequence, not without a sequence."
Investigating "What is the cause of these five aggregates? one sees that they have ignorance and so forth as their cause.
It arises by way of uttering the speech, "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!
It arises while merely prattling, "Oh, what suffering! Oh, what suffering!"
“O Lord of Devas, I say that mental joy (*somanassa*) is of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
Thus it was said; on what account was this said? In this regard, if one should know of a certain mental joy:
“When I cultivate this mental joy, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline,” such [a joy]...
Joy should not be cultivated. In this regard, if one should know of a certain joy:
"When I cultivate this joy, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase," such joy should be cultivated.

In this regard, whether it be accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, or without applied thought and without sustained thought—those [states] which are without applied thought and without sustained thought...
These are more excellent. "O Lord of Devas, I say that joy is of two kinds:
that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated"—this was said with reference to this.

Grief arises for one who reflects, "Alas, I have not been able to perform the invitation for purity (*visuddhi-pavāraṇā*) together with my fellow celibates," and streams of tears flow, as in the case of the Elder Mahāsīva who dwelt in a mountain cave near a village.
"Our teacher is a refuge for others, yet he is unable to provide one for himself; I shall give him instruction.
Thinking thus, he traveled through the air, descended near the monastery, and approached the teacher who was seated in his daytime quarters.
Having performed the proper duties of service, he sat down to one side.
"Why have you come, O alms-collector? he asked.
"There is no need for a blessing from you," [the other] replied, and having flown up into the air, he departed.
[The first thought: "This monk has no business with the scriptures; rather, I have come to be his hook."
Realizing, "Now the opportunity will no longer exist; I shall depart at dawn," he placed his bowl and robes nearby.

Having spent the entire day and the first and middle watches of the night reciting the Dhamma, during the last watch, when one elder had finished receiving the recitation and departed, he took his bowl and robes and went out together with him.

Then, thinking, "The path and fruit will not arise for me on a bed through the four postures; until I have attained Arahantship, I shall neither stretch out my back on a bed nor wash my feet," he raised the bed and set it aside.
"Now, though I have practiced the duties of a recluse for thirty years, I have been unable to reach Arahantship.
Surely there is no path or fruit for me in this present existence; I have gained nothing together with my fellow celibates."
He thought, "I shall perform the invitation ceremony for the sake of purification.
"O Mahāsīvatthera, even the deities play with you; is this truly suitable for you?
Having thus increased his insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). He then said, "Now I shall lie down."
Having attended to the lodging, arranged the bed, and provided water at the washing place,
[the woman] sat on the step of the staircase,
thinking, "I shall wash his feet. She made way for him, saying, "Go ahead, venerable sir," and having approached the elder and paid homage, she knelt before him and said, "I shall wash your feet."
Those most excellent gods,
the glorious Akaniṭṭhas,
while their final existence was proceeding—
"That shall be my dwelling place.
Monks, be my heirs to the Dhamma, not my heirs to material things. I have compassion for you, thinking:
'How may my disciples become heirs to the Dhamma, and not heirs to material things? Yet you, monks, are heirs to material things."
You would not be heirs to the Dhamma; you would be heirs to material things, living as disciples of the Teacher who are heirs to material things and not heirs to the Dhamma.
I too would be one who takes [only] that, an heir to material things, living as a disciple of the Teacher who is an heir to material things and not an heir to the Dhamma.
But you, monks, should be my heirs to the Dhamma, not my heirs to material things.
"You too, by that means, would become heirs to the Dhamma, disciples of the Teacher dwelling as heirs to the Dhamma, not as heirs to material things.
I too, by that means, would not be an heir to material things; I would be a disciple of the Teacher dwelling as an heir to the Dhamma, not as an heir to material things.
Therefore, monks, be my heirs to the Dhamma, not my heirs to material things; I have compassion for you."
"How might my disciples become heirs to the Dhamma, rather than heirs to material things?
Thus they seek out the Blessed One, asking, "Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the God of Gods, the Bull among Men, the Lion among Men?
And it has also been said: "At that time, the Blessed One was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped."
He is honored and receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is also honored... [as before] ...with medicinal requisites for the sick.
Cunda, as far as any Saṅgha or group has arisen in the world at present, I do not see any other single Saṅgha that has attained such excellence in gain and fame as the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, Cunda.”
"Give it to our teacher! Give it to our preceptor! they cried out with loud and great clamor.
This conduct of theirs became known even to the Blessed One. Thereupon, the Blessed One, perceiving it to be improper, felt a sense of spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*) and reflected:

"Since requisites are not allowable, it is not possible to lay down a training rule (*sikkhāpada*). For the practice of the ascetic life for sons of noble family is dependent upon requisites. Well then, I shall teach the way of being an heir to the Dhamma."
It will be like the formulation of training rules for clansmen who desire to train, and like a full-length mirror placed at the city gate;
for just as when a full-length mirror is set at the city gate, the four castes see their own reflections therein,
abandon their faults, and become faultless.
For, brahmin, the Blessed One is the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path;
he is the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the one skilled in the path.

Indeed, friends, the Blessed One knows what should be known and sees what should be seen; he has become vision, he has become knowledge, he has become the Dhamma, he has become Brahmā; he is the speaker.
"The Tathāgata is the proclaimer of the goal, the guide to the Deathless, the giver of the Deathless, and the Lord of Dhamma.
... With his own hands, he served and satisfied him with excellent hard food and soft food.
"Are you not one who rejected even the leftovers of the Sugata’s alms-food, yet now you have conceived such a desire?"
“A monk who is difficult to support cannot be maintained.
Having made the promise, “Our venerable one is easy to support; he is satisfied with even a little; we ourselves will maintain him,” they support him.

[The Teacher says: “Are you indeed the same person who, at that time, having refused even the food left over from the Sugata’s meal, performed the duty of a recluse despite being overcome by hunger and weakness, yet today you are devoted to idleness?”

"But that talk which is conducive to self-effacement, suitable for removing mental hindrances, and leads to complete disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna—namely, talk on fewness of desires...
This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
This brief summary has been recited by me; it has not been explained in detail. [To those] who receive the Dhamma...
"Having learned it, the monks will approach Ānanda or Kaccāna and ask them;
they will explain it by reconciling it with my own knowledge. Then those who have received the Dhamma will ask me again.
To them, I shall say: 'Monks, it was well-spoken by Ānanda; it was well-spoken by Kaccāna. Even if you were to ask me about that same matter, [I would speak in the same way].'"
"I too would explain it in exactly this way.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was staying at Nādikā in the Brick House. Now, at that time... [Cūḷagosiṅgasutta]
At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila were dwelling in the Gosiṅga Sāla-tree grove.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and approached the Gosiṅga Sāla-tree grove.
The keeper of the grove saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Having seen him, he [informed] the Blessed One...
He said this: "Great ascetic, do not enter this park; there are three sons of good family living here who are intent on their own welfare.
Do not cause them discomfort. [I thought: "I shall encourage these sons of good family, uplift them, offer them hospitality, and teach them the Dhamma."

The Venerable Anuruddha heard the park-keeper conversing with the Blessed One. Having heard this, he said to the park-keeper: "Friend park-keeper, do not turn the Blessed One away; our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.
"I am staying here with three people, and there are no other renunciants here at all. Yet this park-keeper is conversing as if with a renunciant; who could this possibly be?"
"This guardian of the estate does not realize that he is conversing with the Supreme Person in the world; he thinks he is conversing with some ordinary monk.
We three live together in harmony. If I were to go out to meet him alone, our communal living would cease to exist.
Therefore, I shall go out to meet him taking my dear friends with me, just as the Blessed One did."
"He is dear to me; likewise, my companions are dear to me. Desiring to go out to meet them together with them, he approached [the Buddha] without having done so himself.
"Venerable sir, this thought occurred to me: 'What if I were to set aside my own mind and [entrust myself] to these very venerable ones?'"
"May we live according to the mind. "Venerable sir, having set aside my own mind, I live according to the minds of these very venerable ones;
for, venerable sir, though our bodies are diverse, we consider our minds to be one.
"Excellent, excellent, Anuruddhas! But, Anuruddhas, do you dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute?"
"Indeed, venerable sir, we dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute.
"But in what way, Anuruddhas, do you dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute?

"Venerable sir, as we dwell thus diligent, ardent, and resolute, have we attained any superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable dwelling? [The Blessed One said: "Anuruddhas, as you dwell thus diligent, ardent, and resolute, have you attained any superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable dwelling?"

"What could we not have, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, as much as we desire, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, we enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
This, venerable sir, is for us who dwell heedful, ardent, and resolute."
"A superhuman state, a distinction in noble knowledge and vision, a comfortable dwelling has been attained.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā*, Sagāthāvagga Saṃyutta,
Yakkhasaṃyutta.
The Āḷavaka Sutta:
Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavī, in the abode of the yakkha Āḷavaka.

Carrying a carrying-pole, he came along to clear himself of the reproach that he had failed to catch a deer; seeing a great banyan tree with thick foliage and leaves not far from the city, he approached its foot to dispel his fatigue.
Whomever there were who were worthy [of the task], with reference to them he said, "Let whoever desires life go forth.

When people heard that the king was catching thieves and handing them over to the *yakkha*, they refrained from committing acts of theft. Subsequently, due to the absence of new thieves and the exhaustion of the old ones, the prisons became empty.
Fearing that people would cause unrest, thinking, "The king is sending us his father and his grandfather," he forbade it, saying, "May this not be pleasing to you."
“Your Majesty, there is no boy in the city except for your son, Prince Āḷavaka, in the inner palace.
Then the yakkha Āḷavaka approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
“Come out, ascetic! “Very well, sir,” the Blessed One replied, and he came out. “Enter, ascetic! “Very well, sir,” the Blessed One replied.
He entered. A second time, the yakkha Āḷavaka said this to the Blessed One: "Come out, ascetic! "Very well, sir," the Blessed One came out.
"Enter, ascetic! "Very well, sir," the Blessed One entered. A third time, the yakkha Āḷavaka said this to the Blessed One:
"Come out, ascetic! "Very well, sir," the Blessed One came out. "Enter..."
"Ascetic! "Friend, you are welcome," the Blessed One said, and he entered. For a fourth time, the yakkha Āḷavaka spoke thus to the Blessed One:
"Come out, ascetic! "I will not come out for you, friend;
do whatever you must do. "I will ask you a question, ascetic; if you do not answer me, either your mind..."
"I will hurl you [away], or I will split your heart, or I will seize you by the feet and hurl you across the Ganges!
"Friend, I do not see anyone in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,
its devas and humans, who could hurl my mind or split my heart, or seize me by the feet and hurl me across the Ganges."
"Throw it across the Ganges. Moreover, friend, ask whatever you doubt.
He replied, "Who is this called 'the Blessed One' who has entered my abode?
[The other said,] "Friend, you do not know our Teacher, the Blessed One, who, while dwelling in the Tusita heaven, performed the five great observations..."

By means of the method beginning with "Having looked," as they spoke up until the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, they described the thirty-two portents at the time of rebirth-linking and so forth, and then challenged him, saying:
"Friend, did you not see these wonders too?
"See now whether your Teacher is of great power, or mine! he said, and stepped with his right foot upon the peak of Mount Kelāsa, which was sixty yojanas in extent.
“Suppose I were to discharge a weapon that is invincible to anyone.

This was said with the following connection: “This ascetic is devoted to dwelling in loving-kindness (*mettā*); well then, having provoked him, I shall separate him from his loving-kindness. Then the Yakkha Āḷavaka approached the Blessed One... [as before] ...“Come out, ascetic!

“This ascetic is indeed easy to speak to; he has come out at a single word! It would have been easy for me to attack this ascetic in battle all night long for no reason at all. Thinking thus, he became soft-hearted and reflected again:
"This ascetic comes out when told to come out; he goes in when told to go in.
Suppose I were to exhaust this ascetic throughout the entire night in this very way, seize him by the feet, and throw him across the Ganges.
Having conceived this evil thought, for the fourth time he said, "Come out, ascetic!"
What indeed is the wealth of a person that is most excellent?
What well-practiced thing brings happiness?
And what indeed is the sweetest of all tastes?
"How does one live the life they call the best?
Faith is the supreme wealth for a person here;
the Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness."
Truth is indeed the sweetest of tastes;
they say that the life of one who lives by wisdom is the best life.
One endowed with faith and perfected in virtue—
Because of the statement: "Endowed with fame and wealth, whatever region he frequents, there indeed he is honored."
By truth even water flows [for one];
by truth the wise destroy even poison;
by truth the rain-god pours down his showers.
Established in truth, they aspire for Nibbāna.
Whatever flavors there are on this earth,
truth is the sweetest of those flavors.
The ascetics and brahmins who stand firm in truth cross to the further shore of birth and death.
How does one cross the flood? How does one cross the ocean?
How does one transcend suffering? How is one purified?
Through faith one crosses the flood; through diligence, the ocean.
Through energy one transcends suffering; through wisdom one is purified.
How does one obtain wisdom? How does one find wealth?
How does one attain fame? How does one bind friends?
And how, having passed from this world to the next world, does one not grieve?
One who has faith in the Dhamma of the Arahants for the attainment of Nibbāna,
being heedful and discerning, gains wisdom through a desire to learn.
One who acts appropriately, bears his burden, and exerts effort finds wealth.
Through truth one attains fame; by giving, one binds friends.
From this world to the next, thus departing, one does not grieve—this is for one in whom these four qualities exist.
For one who has faith, seeks the household life,
possesses truth, self-control, fortitude, and generosity—
he indeed does not grieve after passing away.
Come now, ask others as well—
many recluses and brahmins—
if there are indeed those who possess truth and generosity.
There is even more piercing than anger.
How indeed could I now question the many ascetics and brahmins,
since it is I who today understand that which concerns the life to come?
Truly, for my benefit has the Buddha come to Āḷavī to dwell,
so that today I may understand where a gift given bears great fruit.
Thus shall I wander from village to village, from town to town.
Honoring the Fully Awakened One and the sublime nature of the Dhamma,
[I praise] this prince, who possesses the marks of a hundred merits,
endowed with every limb and perfect in his physical characteristics.
"With an uplifted mind and joyful heart, I give this to you;
accept it for the welfare of the world, O Seer.
"May this prince be long-lived."
And you too, O Yakkha, may you be happy;
remain free from illness for the welfare of the world.
This prince goes for refuge to the Buddha... [and so on] ...to the Dhamma... [and so on] ...to the Saṅgha.
The Commentary on the Mahāvagga Saṃyutta:
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling among the Magadhans at the village of Nālaka, afflicted and suffering from illness.
He was very ill. And the novice Cunda was the attendant of the Venerable Sāriputta. Then the Venerable Sāriputta attained final nibbāna through that very same illness.
Thereupon, the novice Cunda, taking the Venerable Sāriputta’s bowl and robes, went to Sāvatthī, to Jetavana, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika.

He went to the monastery where the Venerable Ānanda was, and having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the novice Cunda said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna; here is his bowl and robe. "There is this, friend..."
“The night has dawned, Cunda; let us go, friend Cunda, to see the Blessed One.
Having approached him, we shall report this matter to the Blessed One. “Very well, venerable sir,” the novice Cunda replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
"Do the Buddhas pass away first, or rather the chief disciples?
"May the Blessed One grant me leave, venerable sir; may the Sugata grant me leave. The time for my final nibbāna has come; I have relinquished the life-faculty.
"Where will you attain final nibbāna, Sāriputta?"
“There is, venerable sir, a rose-apple tree in the village of Nāḷaka in Magadha;
there I shall attain final nibbāna. “Now, Sāriputta, you may think it is the right time. But now, for your elder and younger brothers, such a sight of a bhikkhu as this will be difficult to obtain.
Teach them the Dhamma,” he said. Then the Venerable Ānanda and the novice Cunda approached the Blessed One; having approached...
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, this novice Cunda says: 'Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna;
here is his bowl and robe. Moreover, venerable sir, my body feels as if it were drugged."
Having heard, "The quarters are no longer clear to me, and the teachings do not manifest to me; the Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna," [he said]:
"Even with a small load, the wise and discerning person raises themselves up, like a tiny spark when it is blown upon."
He who has gone forth after abandoning delightful sensual pleasures for five hundred births— him,
free from passion, with well-composed faculties;
Worship Sāriputta who has attained final nibbāna.
Strong in patience, like the earth, he is not disturbed,
nor does he act under the sway of the mind.
Compassionate, merciful, and extinguished—
worship Sāriputta, who has attained final Nibbāna.
Just as a son of a caṇḍāla, having entered the city...
He moves with a humble mind, his hands like a basket;
even so does this Sāriputta dwell.
Pay homage to Sāriputta, who has attained final nibbāna.
Just as a bull with its horns cut off wanders through the village and the forest without causing harm,
so does this Sāriputta dwell.
"Worship Sāriputta who has attained final Nibbāna.
Furthermore, venerable sir, my body feels as if it has become numb.
"Ānanda, has Sāriputta passed away having taken up the aggregate of virtue, or the aggregate of concentration?"
"Or having taken up the aggregate of virtue, he has attained final Nibbāna; or having taken up the aggregate of wisdom, he has attained final Nibbāna;
or having taken up the aggregate of liberation, he has attained final Nibbāna; or having taken up the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, he has attained final Nibbāna.
"Was it not already declared by me, Ānanda, that from all things dear and beloved there must be change, separation, and parting?"
Change, Ānanda—how could that be found here? That what is born, become, conditioned, and subject to dissolution should not dissolve—that is impossible.

"He applies energy with the thought: 'If wholesome states do not arise, that would lead to my harm'; he applies energy with the thought:

The *kolaṃkola* stream-enterer.

And what kind of person is a *kolaṃkola*? Here, a certain person, through the complete destruction of the three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and bound for full enlightenment; having wandered through two or three families, [he will put an end to suffering].
Having wandered through saṃsāra, he makes an end of suffering; this person is called "one who goes from family to family" (kolaṃkolo).
What kind of person is the "one-seeded" (ekabījī) stream-enterer? Here, a certain person, through the total destruction of three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer.
He is one whose nature is not to fall into states of woe, who is fixed and destined for full enlightenment; having produced only one more human existence, he makes an end of suffering.
This is called the person who is a "single-seeder" (*ekabījī*).
(The Description of the Once-returner)
And what kind of person is a once-returner? Here, a certain person, through the complete destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, becomes a once-returner;
returning only once more to this world, he makes an end of suffering. This is called a person who is a once-returner.
